# Recolor matching-color regions using a crossbar

In this demonstrated task pattern, a grid has a thick horizontal/vertical band in color C dividing the canvas. The side/region beyond the band contains many disconnected patches of a single color A, plus some other colors; the band itself is already color B. In the demo, all color-A objects that were on the opposite side of the full-width color-B horizontal bar from the target-side region were recolored to B, while color-A objects on the same side as the bar-associated region remained A. The bar itself and all other colors remained unchanged.

For the task instance demonstrated: a full-width horizontal bar (color 7) sat around row 10, separating rows 0-8 from lower rows. The compact A-color objects (2) above the bar all changed to 7; A objects below the bar remained 2. Other colors were preserved. In another demo, color-A was 8 and crossbar color B was 0; the color-8 objects above the full-width horizontal bar were changed to 0, with lower objects unchanged. This confirms per-instance color substitution based on which side of the separator an object lies, not a fixed palette.

Workflow: identify full-length separator line/band and its color, group same-color patches into objects, infer which side is selected from the demo, recolor only those objects, preserve separator and other colors, validate dimensions and every affected cell. Do not apply fixed colors from these examples without demo evidence.

# Selective recoloring across a full-grid separator

A full-width horizontal bar in color B can divide same-colored object clusters into two groups. In this demonstrated task, the clusters of color A above the bar were recolored to B; clusters of A below it and all unrelated cells/colors were preserved. The separator itself remains unchanged.

Evidence across two demos used different palettes (A=2, B=7 in one; A=8, B=0 in another), so infer colors per instance rather than hardcoding. Find the full-width separator, locate the repeated target-color objects, note which side changes in the demo, and recolor only those objects. Preserve all other cells exactly; validate output size and rows.

name: arc-collinear-marker-connector
description: Use when sparse same-color markers are joined along rows and columns. Fill only gaps between aligned marker pairs with the demonstrated connector color.

# Collinear marker connector

Use when an ARC grid has a uniform background and sparse marker cells, and demonstrations show connector-colored cells appearing along straight rows/columns between markers.

## Rule established for task-63e6a38f
In the observed variant, preserve all original cells and insert color 3 into background cells strictly between aligned pairs of same-color markers in a common row or column. Markers are endpoints and remain unchanged. Use all same-color marker alignments; a line containing multiple markers is partitioned by consecutive markers, and each gap is filled. Do not extend past the outermost endpoint, fill diagonals, globally recolor the background, or connect different marker colors. If there are no background cells between a pair (adjacent endpoints), no additional cells change.

Evidence across demos: demo 1 had background 6 and marker color 5; output color 3 traced horizontal and vertical gaps between aligned 5 markers while leaving unbounded background outside marker endpoints unchanged. Demo 2 had background 9, markers 1, and likewise filled gaps with 3 (e.g. along rows with multiple 1 endpoints), retaining marker cells and background not lying between aligned markers. Demo 3 used background 5 and marker 7, with the same connector color 3 and horizontal/vertical gap fills. In the accepted test, color-8 markers at row 1, columns 12 and 14 caused only the intervening cell (row 1, column 13) to become 3; the other marker cells and background were unchanged.

## Application and validation
1. Copy the input grid.
2. For every row and every column, gather positions of marker cells (the non-background color) in sorted order.
3. Between consecutive marker positions, change only the intervening background cells to connector color 3.
4. Preserve markers and all cells outside these gaps. Validate dimensions and palette.

Infer the palette from current demos; do not assume the marker/background/connector colors remain fixed on task-ID recurrence unless confirmed. Keep the strict action-JSON output protocol in ARC stream tasks.

2. Infer background and marker colors from the current instance's demos; connector color was 3 in the observed task variant.
3. For every row and column, gather marker positions in sorted order.
4. Between consecutive marker positions, change only intervening background cells to the connector color.
5. Preserve markers and all cells outside gaps. Validate dimensions and palette.

Infer the palette from current demos; do not assume colors remain fixed on task-ID recurrence unless confirmed. Keep the strict action-JSON output protocol in ARC stream tasks.

---
name: arc-collinear-marker-connector
description: Use when aligned markers appear connected by filled gaps.
---

# Collinear marker connector

Use when an ARC grid has a uniform background and sparse marker cells, and demonstrations show connector-colored cells appearing along straight rows or columns between markers.

## Rule established for task-63e6a38f
Preserve all original cells and insert color 3 into background cells strictly between aligned pairs of same-color markers in a common row or column. Markers are endpoints and remain unchanged. Use all same-color marker alignments; a line with multiple markers is partitioned by consecutive markers, and each gap is filled. Do not extend past the outermost endpoint, fill diagonals, globally recolor the background, or connect different marker colors. Adjacent endpoints need no inserted cells.

Evidence across the three demos: demo 1 had background 6 and marker color 5; output color 3 traced horizontal and vertical gaps between aligned 5 markers while leaving background outside marker endpoints unchanged. Demo 2 had background 9, markers 1, and likewise filled gaps with 3, retaining marker cells and unrelated background. Demo 3 used background 5 and marker 7, with the same connector color 3 and horizontal/vertical gap fills. In the accepted test, color-8 markers at row 1, columns 12 and 14 caused only the intervening cell (row 1, column 13) to become 3; all other cells were unchanged. A further accepted 21x8 test used background 7, marker 8, connector 3. Fill every strict gap between consecutive same-color markers in every row and column, preserving marker endpoints and all cells outside such gaps. This included multi-marker lines: row 3's markers at columns 2 and 7 filled columns 3-6; column 2's markers at rows 3, 8, and 20 filled rows 4-7 and 9-19. Crossings where horizontal and vertical gaps overlap remain connector color 3. No extrapolation past outer endpoints.

## Confirmed recurring variant: task-041f67cf
This variant uses sparse same-color markers on a uniform background and inserts color 2 strictly between consecutive aligned markers, preserving marker endpoints and all other cells. Demo: in each row of a 25x4 grid, color-4 markers at columns 0 and 2 had the intervening color-7 cell changed to 2; rows without marker pairs were unchanged. Accepted test: background 6, markers 8; row 4 had markers at columns 5, 7, 9, so columns 6 and 8 became 2; row 13 had markers at columns 2 and 4, so column 3 became 2. Everything else stayed unchanged. This supports connecting consecutive aligned same-color markers horizontally and vertically with color 2; do not extend beyond endpoints. Infer palette from current demos, as connector color varies by task variant.

### Accepted task-041f67cf test (18x27; background 5, marker 7, connector 2)
The test was accepted using the same strict orthogonal-gap rule. Recolor only background cells strictly between consecutive aligned color-7 markers to 2; preserve marker endpoints and every other cell. In this grid, the only active alignments were horizontal: row 5 (0-indexed) had markers at columns 3 and 5, so column 4 became 2; row 15 had markers at columns 9,11,13,15,17,19,21, so columns 10,12,14,16,18,20 became 2; row 17 had markers at columns 14,16,18, so columns 15 and 17 became 2. No vertical marker pair occurred. This provides accepted evidence for marker/background palette 7/5 and confirms applying the rule only to actual gaps, not extending beyond endpoints.

### Further accepted task-041f67cf instance (2026-09)
Demo used background 9, marker 6, and connector 2. In rows 9, 10, 11, 20, 21, 23, and 26, any color-6 markers separated by exactly one background cell were joined by changing only that intervening cell to 2. Specifically: row 9 markers c1,c3; rows 10 and 11 markers c0,c2; rows 20 and 21 markers c1,c3; row 23 markers c1,c3,c5 (fill c2,c4); row 26 markers c0,c2. No vertical connector cells were needed in this demo. The accepted test had background 7 and marker 4, with connector 2: fill only strict horizontal gaps between consecutive markers in each row (r1: c2,c4; r6: c3; r8: c5,c7,c9,c11), leaving all other cells unchanged. This confirms horizontal consecutive-marker gap filling with a stable connector color 2 across palettes; still preserve all endpoints and avoid extension beyond them. Check vertical alignments too where present, as supported by the other task-041f67cf evidence.

## Confirmed recurring variant: task-381e5135
The sparse color-3 markers in a mostly color-6 field identify horizontal/vertical gaps, filled with color 2. Preserve all original cells, including all marker 3s and background; only fill cells strictly between consecutive aligned markers. Demo: background 6, markers 3, connector 2. Horizontal row 7 markers at columns 0,1,2 and 6: fill columns 3-5; row 11 markers at columns 0 and 6: fill columns 1-5; row 12 markers at columns 0,2,4,6: fill columns 1,3,5. Vertical alignments include col0 markers rows 7,10,11 (fill rows 8-9 between 7 and 10), and col6 markers rows 7,9,11 (fill rows 8 and 10). In the 30x27 test (background 7, marker 5, connector 2), this rule was accepted; same behavior with palette inferred from current demo. Note missing cells in col19/25 or row23 are not bridged unless there are aligned marker endpoints on both sides. Do not extend beyond endpoints or fill arbitrary enclosed-region/background gaps.

## task-381e5135 generated variants and unresolved instance (2026-09)
Do not assume this task ID always means straight collinear connector fills. It has multiple variants. The classic marker-connector recurrence is separately confirmed: same-color sparse markers in rows/columns have only intervening background cells filled with connector color 2. However, the current failed 24x21 test had demos from several structures and all 8 submissions were wrong; none of the guesses below are validated output.

Current instance demos (palette varies) reveal a common operation of changing selected background-colored cells to 2 along selected rows/columns, but plain interpolation between consecutive same-color markers does not account for all cells:

- Pair 2, 13x15, bg8, markers0. Changes: row0 c1,c3-6; col1 r1-2,r4-5,r8-9; col7 r4-5,r9; row10 c5-6. Not all aligned marker gaps are filled.

A fresh 23x24 demonstration confirms the classic strict orthogonal connector rule exactly: retain marker color 4 and background 1; insert 3 into every cell strictly between consecutive same-color markers in each row and column. A cell-by-cell replay of that single demo matched the provided output exactly, including multiple-marker rows/columns and intersections. 2. Infer background and marker colors from the current instance's demos; connector color was 3 in the observed task variant.

# Selective recoloring across a separator

A full-width horizontal bar in color B can divide same-colored object clusters into two groups. In this demonstrated task, the clusters of color A above the bar were recolored to B; clusters of A below it and all unrelated cells/colors were preserved. The separator itself remains unchanged.

Evidence across two demos used different palettes (A=2, B=7 in one; A=8, B=0 in another), so infer colors per instance rather than hardcoding. Find the full-width separator, locate the repeated target-color objects, note which side changes in the demo, and recolor only those objects. Preserve all other cells exactly; validate output size and rows.

## Confirmed distinct separator-parallel stripe/adjacency variant: task-67762d72
Do not confuse this with the recoloring variant above. Across three demos, a full-length color-2 separator (horizontal or vertical) remained unchanged, and a new full-length color-8 stripe was added parallel to it. A nearby non-background object was repositioned so it abutted the new stripe; preserve its color and silhouette. The side occupied by the object relative to the new stripe varies, so derive orientation and translation from the example rather than assuming it is always above/left. Demos: (1) 17x22 horizontal 2 row index 3; isolated 5 at (10,16) moved to (4,16), and row index 5 became all 8, placing the object immediately above the stripe. (2) 22x22 vertical 2 col index 20; color-4 block in cols18-19 stayed in place and full 8 stripe was added at col17, immediately beside it. (3) 16x28 vertical 2 col index 12; full 8 stripe added at col17, and the color-3 pattern was translated left so its right edge abutted col17 while preserving shape. Accepted test: 18x22 horizontal 2 row index15; color-7 motif translated down two rows (from rows7-12 to rows9-14), and full 8 stripe added at row8 immediately above it. Other background and separator cells were preserved. Apply this only when demos support this family; it is a distinct variant despite sharing a separator with crossbar recoloring.

## Confirmed distinct separator-plus-outward-stripe variant (task-67762d72 demos)
A full-width color-2 horizontal separator is preserved. Locate the non-background object on one side; preserve its cells and position, then add a full-width color-8 stripe immediately beyond the object's far edge (on the side away from the separator). Demo 1: separator row 1; color-3 irregular object spans rows 2–12; add stripe row 13. Demo 2: separator row 4; color-0 segment is at row 5; add stripe row 6. Unlike the other separator-parallel variant above, the motif is not moved; the added stripe is placed adjacent to its far edge. ---
name: arc-demo-action-budget
description: Use when ARC demos cost actions. Synthesize before acting.
---

# Demo and action-budget discipline for ARC streams

Use this class-level workflow whenever an ARC interface charges for demo requests or wrong submissions.

## Before requesting a demo
1. Audit every demonstration already received: enumerate exact input/output differences using consistent coordinates and note relevant preserved lookalikes.
2. Separate the transformation itself (e.g., recolor, extend, crop) from the selector (which cells/objects are affected) and extent/phase (exactly how much changes). A demo may establish the operation but not the selector.
3. Form at least two concrete candidate rules that fit all examples so far. State how each would differ on the test and identify a feature a further demo could reveal.
4. Request another demo only if that discriminator is likely to occur and resolving it could change the test output enough to justify its cost. If candidates/predictions cannot be stated concretely, continue analyzing current evidence instead of reflexively requesting.

## After each returned demo
Pause before the next action. Compare input and output cell-by-cell; record the full diff, including unchanged counterexamples/lookalikes. State what the pair rules in or rules out and whether it distinguishes the candidates. Repeated examples of a broad visual pattern do not prove an unresolved selector or exact fill extent. Do not chain demo requests without this synthesis.

## Before submission
- Replay the candidate transformation against every demo, including preserved cells.
- Preserve unrelated structure and validate output dimensions, row lengths, coordinate bounds, and palette.
- If evidence is incomplete, do not treat a plausible guess as validated. Weigh another demo against its cost and the remaining submission budget.
- After incorrect feedback, materially reassess the rule and its unsupported assumptions rather than making near-identical speculative edits.
- In strict action protocols, emit exactly one allowed JSON action and no commentary.

## Pitfalls
- Using sequential demo requests as a substitute for analysis; this can consume budget while leaving the test selector unresolved.
- Confusing confidence in the broad transformation with confidence in which test cells it applies to.
- Failing to track changed and preserved examples at exact coordinates.

# Strict ARC action-only workflow

In action protocols that require exactly one puzzle action per reply, keep the whole interaction within that contract. After a demo arrives, inspect changed and preserved cells internally, decide whether it discriminates current hypotheses, then emit exactly one of the allowed puzzle actions. Do not insert task-list/planning calls or unrelated tools between demo feedback and the next puzzle action. Before requesting a further demo, specify internally at least two plausible rules with different test predictions and a concrete property the next example could distinguish; otherwise synthesize existing evidence and choose the best supported action. This prevents spending demo budget without reducing uncertainty and avoids malformed protocol turns.

# Reduced output from patterned grids: establish the encoding before submitting

A 30x30 Continual-ARC instance (task-5186866a) supplied four demos where each input contained a prominent region of color 8 and the output was a much smaller grid (demo outputs 4x4, 4x5, 9x4, and 3x7). The test also had a 9x3 block of 8s. This looked like a missing/occluded patch, and guesses extracted cells from the opposite side or reflected neighboring rows. Those guesses were rejected; the session ended unresolved.

Lesson: matching the output dimensions to the colored mask/region is not evidence that output equals the hidden contents, a mirrored patch, or an adjacent crop. The four examples varied in their relationships, and no candidate was replayed cell-by-cell across them before the test guesses. For future reduced-output tasks:

1. Identify the exact output-sized candidate regions in every demo, including possible transforms (flips/rotations), reductions, and pattern decoding.
2. Compare each candidate against the *entire* demonstrated output, coordinate by coordinate; include preserved surrounding patterns and repeated structures as possible source clues.
3. Keep extraction, selector, orientation, and any mapping/recoloring as separate hypotheses. Eliminate candidates that fail even one demo.
4. If multiple interpretations still predict different test outputs, spend a demo only when a concrete discriminator is identified. Do not use a test submission as a probe for an unvalidated crop guess, especially after prior rejections.
5. Treat the task-5186866a answer as unresolved: none of its crop/reflection test guesses was accepted, and no rule was confirmed.

This is a process lesson, not a solved transformation. It should not be used to infer a particular crop rule from a task ID or from color 8 alone.

Pointer: see the class-level reduced-grid workflow in `arc-demo-rule-inference` and the action discipline in this skill.

# Periodic patterns interrupted by zero patches

When a grid shows a repeating color sequence around one or more rectangular zero regions, do not automatically treat the zeros as missing pixels. First classify each patch as an occlusion or a true structural blank by examining repeated phase and surrounding geometry. Derive candidate periods and phase only from intact regions, then compare predictions cell-for-cell with each demo output. Explicitly inspect zero patches that remain zero in a demo: they are counterexamples to blanket restoration and may signal a semantic boundary, a separate panel, or an intentionally empty region. On the test, restore only patches whose role is supported by the demonstrations; never assume continuation merely because it makes the global pattern look regular.

## Failure lesson
A candidate based on global periodic continuation can fit most cells and still fail if it fills a zero region that the task preserves. After any rejection, reassess patch role and the full output mask rather than trying another phase/palette variant. Prioritize changed-versus-preserved patch geometry, not only sequence regularity.

# Post-demo synthesis and action gate

After every demo return, pause before choosing another action. Compare input and output cell-by-cell; note the exact changed cells and relevant unchanged lookalikes, then state which hypotheses are ruled in/out and whether the example distinguishes candidate predictions on the test. Do not request another demo until this synthesis is complete and a concrete unresolved distinction remains that another example could clarify. If the exact diff or its implication is unclear, keep analyzing rather than spending a demo.

In strict action-only ARC interfaces, the next reply after a demo should contain exactly one authorized puzzle-action JSON object. Do not interleave unrelated terminal/date checks, planning tools, or extra skill/tool calls after receiving a demo; load relevant guidance before puzzle play when possible, then synthesize the demo and act.

# Recovery after rejected predictions in demo-limited ARC

Use when a test output is rejected but additional submissions remain.

1. Treat incorrect feedback as evidence against the inferred rule, not only a possible typo.
2. Separate the broad operation from its selector and exact extent. Demos may show that some objects are recolored without revealing which test objects qualify.
3. Before another submission, state the unsupported assumptions in the rejected answer and enumerate changed and preserved structures across every demo.
4. Propose a materially distinct predicate that explains both positive and negative examples, then replay its complete output against each demo. Changing only the colors on the same guessed test targets is not a new hypothesis.
5. If no predicate reproduces every demo, do not make ad hoc local edits. Request another demo only if it separates explicit candidate rules and is worth its cost. When demos are exhausted, weigh the remaining attempt cost against the evidence; do not present an unsupported selector as validated.

Keep exact coordinates, dimensions, and output shape under audit. This recovery gate complements the broader changed/preserved audit and demo-request discipline.

# Strict ARC action-only response workflow

In a Continual-ARC interaction where every turn requires exactly one action JSON:

1. Load relevant ARC guidance before puzzle play if feasible.
2. After a demo response, do not reflexively request another demo. First compare the returned input/output at fixed coordinates and identify all changed cells, the operation, its selector, its extent, and informative preserved lookalikes.
3. Record internally which test predictions are supported and what uncertainty remains. A demo request should be justified by a specific discriminator likely to change the test answer.
4. Avoid unrelated tools, no-op calls, or repeated skill lookups after receiving a puzzle demo. They consume attention without satisfying the required reasoning step. Analyze from visible data, then choose one authorized action.
5. Output exactly one valid JSON action and no prose. Revalidate grid dimensions and row lengths before submission.

Pitfall: repeated demo requests without synthesizing returned examples can exhaust the demo budget while leaving the task unresolved. Another pitfall is spending the post-demo turn on tools that do not analyze the grid; the appropriate next step is the ARC action itself after internal synthesis.

This reference captures process guidance only; it does not establish a transformation rule for task-5186866a, whose test remained unresolved in the observed session.

This is specifically a warning against assuming every diagonal marker or every same-color pair activates a ray.

Demo evidence (0-indexed):
- Demo 1 (9x9, bg4): 1 markers at (2,1) and (7,6); output draws a bounded down-right 1 diagonal joining them, adding (3,2),(4,3),(5,4),(6,5). No 6 marker present.
- Demo 2 (8x11, bg8): 6 at (3,4) is extended along its NW-SE diagonal to both boundaries (from (0,1) through (7,8)); 1s at (1,6),(6,1) are joined on their down-left/up-right diagonal by filling (2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2). Note that the 1 connector crosses a location that was background and is not the 6 ray's same coordinate line in this orientation.
- Demo 3 (9x12, bg4): 1s at (1,7),(7,1) are joined along down-left diagonal, filling (2,6) through (6,2). The 6 at (6,7) remains unchanged, a counterexample to extending every 6 marker.
- Demo 4 (15x12, bg5): output adds diagonal 1/6 cells along several lines, preserving all original markers. For example 1 pair at (3,1),(9,7) is joined down-right through rows 4–8; there are also 6 marker/ray structures, including a long down-left progression from near the top-right to the lower-left edge and another reaching from a lower marker toward an edge. This demo is not sufficient to identify which 6 directions activate; audit the original pair cell-by-cell before generalizing.
- Demo 5 (15x16, bg8): 1 markers at (2,2),(3,12),(11,11),(14,3) and 6 markers at (1,8),(9,9),(10,1),(14,13). Output connects the first two 1 markers down-right across rows 2–3; extends some 1/6 diagonal patterns but leaves other plausible continuations absent. In particular a 6 line through (9,9) is extended up-right/down-left along its diagonal; 6 at (1,8) proceeds down-right; 6 at (10,1) extends down-left to the edge; and the marker (14,13) remains without a conspicuous continuation. This mixed activation is a crucial negative constraint.

Test (19x16, bg4) markers: 1s at (2,2),(4,14),(10,10),(17,9); 6s at (4,4),(6,6),(7,14),(15,2). Eight rejected submissions tried: (1) connecting 1s/rays only in intuitive SE directions; (2) blanket full anti-diagonal 6 lines plus 1 line; (3) only bounded aligned 1 and 6 pairs; (4) full 6 diagonals in another orientation; (5) main-diagonal 1/6 continuation guesses; (6) broad bidirectional 6 rays; (7) bounded marker linking / mixed ray selection; (8) broad diagonal 6 completion plus bounded 1 link. None is validated, and failures indicate selector/direction assumptions—not merely palette or grid dimensions—were unsupported. On recurrence, tabulate every changed and preserved diagonal line in each demo with exact orientation, endpoints, nearest object relationships, and edge direction; derive a selector replaying all five before submitting. If no such rule is established, avoid recycling guesses; demos have a cost and the test attempt cap is finite.

name: arc-demo-rule-inference
description: Use when inferring ARC transformations from demonstrations.
---

# ARC demonstration-driven rule inference

Use for ARC tasks where a test grid is accompanied by one or more demonstrations. Infer a transformation that generalizes, rather than matching a visual hunch.

## Procedure

1. **Parse the full instance.** Record dimensions, distinct colors, repeated backgrounds, exceptional shapes/markers, and any action/attempt/demo caps. Keep row/column coordinates explicit and use them consistently.
2. **Compare each demo cell-by-cell.** Align input and output at matching coordinates when dimensions match. List changed coordinates and their before/after colors; separately note additions, removals, recolorings, dimension changes, and preserved seed structures. If dimensions differ, identify segmentation or object-count mappings that explain the change.
3. **Form a small set of competing rules.** Consider geometry, relative position, orientation, counts, symmetry, lines/regions, and transparency. Do not infer an anchor, target color, or direction solely from visual resemblance.
4. **Replay candidates on the demo.** Apply each candidate to the full demo input and compare every output cell and dimension exactly. Reject rules that leave changes unexplained or predict changes in preserved cells. All demos should fit one rule, aside from supported parameter changes such as color or size.
5. **Use demonstrations economically.** A demo request has a cost. Request one only when a specific unresolved ambiguity could materially change the test output. First extract all constraints from existing examples and test concrete hypotheses; do not request merely because the rule is not immediately obvious.
6. **Apply the validated rule to the test.** Preserve unrelated cells unless demonstrations show otherwise. Verify bounds, row and column counts, allowed values, and output dimensions before submission.

## Unresolved selective-object recoloring stream task task-4902da4a
This task family has varied grid sizes and palettes; each demo output is same dimensions and differs by recoloring a localized connected object/component, while many other objects and even same-color components stay untouched. Never use global palette substitution or infer a fixed target/replacement color. Observed demo changes (1-indexed): pair 1, a 3-cell color-4 object at rows 2-3, cols 24-25 becomes 9; pair 2, a 4-cell color-9 object at rows 5-7, cols 19-20 becomes 0; pair 3, one color-8 cell at row 25, col 12 becomes 9; pair 4, a vertical three-cell color-4 object at rows 19-21, col 4 becomes 1; pair 5, three adjacent color-9 cells at row 5, cols 2-4 become 8; pair 6, the connected color-9 object around rows 6-11, cols 7-10 becomes 0; pair 7, the isolated color-0 cell at row 4, col 15 becomes 2; pair 8, the small color-5 component at rows 9-12, cols 16-17 becomes 8. The common selector/replacement mechanism was not identified from these examples; these local recolorings do not establish a simple color, size, edge, or line-alignment rule. In this task attempt, eight demos were exhausted and all eight test submissions were incorrect. The submitted guesses variously recolored test color-5 motifs or isolated cells to 1, 6, or 8, and finally changed an isolated 0 to 2; none are supported by the demonstrations. Future instances should first build a complete connected-component table for every demo (changed and preserved objects, colors, silhouette, area, location, adjacency and possible paired objects), test a selector and output-color key that explains every pair, and avoid submitting without a rule that replays all examples. This note is a cautionary unresolved case, not a validated rule.

## Confirmed denoising variant: task-16b1bf1f
Images are mostly solid/rectangular coherent regions on a dominant background, with isolated one-cell foreign-color noise and occasional notches in a coherent shape. Clean by changing every isolated anomalous pixel to the underlying region color if it lies inside/on a coherent object; otherwise change it to the background. Preserve coherent regions even when their color is uncommon. Do not globally substitute palette colors, and do not assume the outlier's color predicts its destination.

First demo (22x25, background 4) confirms: remove isolated noise of colors 1,6,7 at coordinates (0-indexed) (0,6),(0,24),(2,0),(2,24),(1,12),(4,13),(4,21),(8,0),(9,21),(10,1),(10,3),(12,7),(12,10),(12,18),(11,21),(15,10),(16,5),(17,7),(21,9); each becomes its local coherent-region/background color. Also fill the anomalous notch (15,10) in a 3-region to 3. Retain solid coherent 3 and 5 objects and small 2x2/rectangular forms, including apparently unusual components. This rule was independently confirmed in three earlier demos: demo 1 (27x10, bg1) removed scattered colors 0/2/3/8/9 and restored cells inside color-6 forms to 6; demo 2 (13x28, bg5) removed singleton intrusions 1/6/9 in coherent color-4 and color-2 regions; demo 3 (12x26, bg5) removed isolated 2/3/4/6 artifacts while preserving coherent 7/8/9 structures.

The accepted test output for the 18x24 grid retained coherent color-5 and color-9 regions plus coherent color-8/9 blocks. It corrected isolated noise as follows (0-indexed): (0,1) 8→2; (2,12) 4→2; (3,2) 1→2; (4,5) 6→2; (7,7) 6→2; (7,20) 4→2; (8,3) 4→2; (8,9) 8→2; (9,14) 4→2; (9,17) 0→2; (9,23) 0→2; (10,4) 3→5; (10,7) 6→5; (10,9) 6→2; (10,16) 6→2; (10,21) 4→2; (13,4) 3→5; (14,11) 8→2; (16,11) 4→9; (16,23) 6→2; (17,1) 6→2. Notably, row 3 col 2 (value 1) and row 10 col 4/value3 and row13 col4/value3 were restored differently according to whether they intrude on a coherent region or lie at its boundary/background. Previous guesses that changed coherent-block extents or left artifacts untouched were wrong. Use local underlying structure and exact changed/preserved audit; validate every cell of the proposed output. Preserve connected/block-shaped objects such as the 1 regions and 8 forms.

### Additional accepted task-16b1bf1f test confirmation (29x13)
A further test was accepted with the same local denoising rule. Background was color 8; coherent regions included a 7 rectangle at rows 0–4, cols 4–9; a 7 block at rows 9–15, cols 10–12; and a 4 block at rows 25–27, cols 8–12. Preserve those full solid forms, including unusual color 4. Correct isolated noise to local structure/background: (0,0) 3→8; (1,7) 3→7; (2,9) 2→7; (4,6) 2→7; (4,12) 9→8; (5,8) 9→8; (7,7) 9→8; (8,11) 2→8; (9,3) 5→8; (9,9) 5→8; (10,5) 3→8; (12,12) 9→7; (13,3) 5→8; (14,7) 3→8; (15,3) 3→8; (15,11) 2→7; (16,1) 5→8; (16,6) 2→8; (16,12) 2→8; (18,6) 3→8; (18,11) 5→8; (19,4) 3→8; (21,0) 9→8; (22,4) 2→8; (24,5) 2→8; (24,9) 2→8; (25,1) 2→8; (27,5) 9→8; (28,8) 9→8. This independently confirms that singleton foreign-colored pixels are noise even when their colors occur elsewhere, while the contiguous 4 block and rectangular 7 regions must remain intact. The accepted output had no other changes.

## Unresolved split-panel reduction: task-9a9d9fc4
A distinct instance had a full-height divider column (color 2) separating 10×27 and 10×27 panels; another demo had a full-width divider row (color 9) separating two 5×14 panels. Outputs were 27×10 and 5×14 respectively, i.e. one panel-sized output, predominantly color 4 with sparse color-3 cells. Inputs used panel colors {8,4} and {7,4} in the vertical-separator demo, and {5,4} above / {2,4} below in the horizontal-separator demo. Test was 18×23 with a full-height color-8 divider at column 11, panels 18×11 using {0,6} and {0,9}; likely output shape 18×11. Eight test submissions all failed. Guesses that treated one panel as a direct binary mask, guessed 3/4 cellwise patterns, or used unrelated hand-built marker placements were not validated. Do not reuse any guessed test grid or assume which half controls the sparse 3s. On recurrence, align both panels to the output, tabulate all coordinates for each input color and each output color in both demos, and test a joint positional relation (including flips/rotations, overlap, and counts) against every output cell before submitting. The rule remains unresolved.
7. **Follow the interface exactly.** In ARC stream tasks requiring a final-line JSON action, emit exactly one valid action object on the last line, without explanatory prose.

## Additional confirmed task-fce33c1b diagonal-residue run (demo + accepted 20x20 test)
Demo 1 was a 10x10 grid whose output is a full periodic pattern using invariant `c-r mod 3` with residue palette `[3,7,3]`: every cell in residue 1 becomes 7, and the other residues become 3. The input's 7 markers lie on a down-right diagonal (`c-r ≡ 1 mod 3`), while sparse 3 clues corroborate the other residues. The accepted 20x20 test used the *other* diagonal orientation, invariant `r+c mod 4`, with palette `[5,3,7,1]` for residues 0,1,2,3 respectively. The clue lines confirmed this: 7 on `r+c ≡2`, 1 on `r+c≡3`, 3 on `r+c≡1`, and 5 on `r+c≡0`. Correct output is `palette[(r+c)%4]` at every cell, including recoloring/removing the sparse input markers into their class color. This run confirms orientation and period must be inferred from current clue geometry; same task can use `c-r` in demos and `r+c` on the test. Validate every clue by its invariant before building the complete grid.

## task-351b5301 failed-submission recovery
This instance is a split-panel non-background occupancy overlap, confirmed by its demo: full vertical separator divides two equal-width panels; output is panel-sized, with 2 iff both aligned cells are nonzero, else 0. On a 17x25 test split at column 12, the output is 17x12. The first submitted answer applied the correct rule but its several marks were shifted by one row; it was rejected. After indexing carefully (0-based), the resubmission aligned panel row r with test input row r, excluding only the separator. Lesson: following an incorrect output that seems rule-consistent, audit coordinate transcription and row alignment before replacing the inferred rule or spending a demo request.

## Confirmed recurring binary-noise palette remapping case
A Continual-ARC instance with dense binary noise on 9/5 was solved by a whole-grid color substitution: every 9 became 0 and every 5 became 9. Its confirming small demo had a 14x5 grid of 9s with one 5; output changed every 9 to 0 and the lone 5 to 9. An earlier demo in the same instance used colors 5/7 and mapped 5→7, 7→0, so do not assume a fixed mapping from color identity alone across palette variants; derive the mapping from the instance's demonstrations and verify it applies globally to every cell. Prior incorrect attempts came from reversing/guessing the 5/9 mapping. For this demonstrated 5/9 variant, use 9→0 and 5→9.

## Confirmed task-8b275e8f run: global binary palette remapping
One 28x26 demo and accepted 21x11 test establish a cellwise global substitution for this instance: every input 5 becomes 3, and every input 3 becomes 0. No other colors occurred. The transformation preserves dimensions and positions; apply it to every cell, not just isolated/connected components or selected patterns. On recurrence, still infer the mapping from current demos rather than assuming this palette mapping is invariant across generated variants. The accepted test contained only 5 and 3 and was exactly the global 5→3, 3→0 remapping.

## Additional confirmed task-fce33c1b run: horizontal periodic stripe completion
A distinct accepted run used full-width monochrome horizontal stripes with blank rows as missing members of a periodic sequence. Fill every row with its sequence color, making each row monochrome; infer orientation, smallest compatible period, residue colors and phase from the current instance's demos. Do not conflate it with diagonal-residue periodic-grid variants under the same ID. In one accepted 28x28 test, known input rows (0-indexed) were r0=4, r7=9, r8=6, r11=1, r21=6, r22=3. Correct output repeated period-6 row sequence `[4,9,6,6,3,1]` across columns, exactly matching all clues. A 16x16 demo had horizontal stripe sequence `[7,6,5,5,3,8]` repeated every six rows. A 4x4 demo alternated rows 9 and 4 after filling two blank rows. A separate diagonal demo is a different variant: infer horizontal-vs-diagonal orientation from current clue geometry, not task ID alone.
A separate recurrence was accepted with sparse/incorrect horizontal stripe colors completed to a repeating row-color sequence. Infer stripe orientation and period from this instance's demos; task ID and prior diagonal cases do not fix either. Demos in this run: (1) 7x7 input had full rows `[0,7,6,6,3,2,4]`; output `[4,7,6,6,3,2,4]`, consistent with period 6 and sequence `[4,7,6,6,3,2]`. (2) Sparse down-right diagonal 9s produced a uniform 9 grid; treat as instance-specific and not evidence to fill unknown residues with 9 in another run. (3) 21x21 sparse horizontal rows 2,8,4,0,0,0,2,0,...,7,...,4,...,4,2 became the repeated period-8 sequence `[2,8,4,4,2,7,2,4]`. Accepted 4x4 test rows `[0,4,4,6]` became `[6,4,4,6]`, consistent with period 3 sequence `[6,4,4]`. Preserve phase and fill/correct rows according to the demo-derived repeat. Determine a period valid against every clue, replay demos, and do not assume a period from task ID or transfer the separate diagonal-residue rule's uncertain missing-class guesses.

## Confirmed recurring case: task-5c4cb9ae (18x18 to 6x6 mini-grid)
Partition the input into a regular grid of 3x3 tiles (not 6x6 tiles). Emit one output cell per tile, preserving tile row/column order. For each tile, ignore background/noise colors 0 and 5; if any other color is present, output that color, otherwise output 0. The demonstrated/test instance had a sole color-4 motif confined to the top-left 6x6 region: it landed in output tile row 0, column 1, producing [[0,4,0,0,0,0], then five all-zero rows]. This was accepted. An initial wrong attempt used 6x6 tiles and produced a 3x3 grid, so carefully distinguish tile size from output dimensions: 18x18 becomes 6x6 via 3x3 tiles. Validate all tile cells, including multi-color exceptional cells if present; the known instance only had color 4 among colors other than 0/5.

## Verified recurring case: task-a613028a (3x2 mirror tiling)
This task family expands any HxW input into a 3H x 2W output by mirror-tiling the original grid. For the demo 3x13 -> 9x26, each source row is expanded horizontally as `reverse(row) + row`; vertically the rows follow `[r3,r2,r1, r1,r2,r3, r3,r2,r1]`. This corresponds to three alternating mirrored row blocks. Equivalently, output `[R][C] = input[vertical_source(R)][horizontal_source(C)]`, with horizontal indices `W-1..0, 0..W-1`; vertical indices `H-1..0, 0..H-1, H-1..0`. Expanded dimensions are 3H by 2W. A separate accepted instance of this task id had a 2x14 test and 6x28 output, consistent with the same dimensional rule. Validate every output row length and total row count before submission; in a 10x14 test, expected dimensions are 30x28. Prior attempt grids for the 10x14 test were malformed (wrong row lengths and/or count) as well as not reliable evidence of a rule failure; the mirror-tiling rule itself matches the demo exactly. The accepted example from the related run was for input `[[2,7,2,2,7,7,2,7,2,2,2,0,2,2],[0,0,7,7,7,7,2,2,7,7,7,2,0,7]]`, output dimensions 6x28.

This task family can change dimensions substantially and is not a same-size recoloring. Do not overfit output dimensions to the demo; apply the 3H x 2W rule and audit exact coordinates, all rows, and all columns.


## Additional task-21fede32 run (unresolved; do not treat guesses as rules)
A separate 14x23 test instance used 8 demos and all 8 submissions failed. All pairs retained dimensions and changed one connected component, but a selector/recolor mapping was not established. Demo changed component → replacement (coordinates 1-indexed):
1. Input 28x16, bg0, color2 separator L at col5 rows1-9 and row9 cols1-5: color5 component rows17-19 cols5-6, silhouette 5/55/05 →2. Many other 5 components unchanged.
2. Input 16x25, bg3, color8 separator L at col4 rows1-4 and row4 cols1-4: isolated 1 at row11 col4 →8. Other 1,6,7,2,9,5 objects unchanged.
3. Input 26x10, bg9, color5 separator L at col5 rows1-6 and row6 cols1-5: color1 component rows11-13 cols4-6 →5. Other objects unchanged.
4. Input 25x27, bg5, color7 separator L at col19 rows1-5 and row5 cols19-27: color2 upper-right component rows6-8 cols21-25 →7. Other color2 and colored objects unchanged.
5. Input 17x21, bg3, no obvious large divider: color4 vertical triplet at col12 rows8-10 →0. Other color4 objects unchanged.
6. Input 15x24, bg8, color0 separator L at col17 rows1-6 and row6 cols17-24: isolated 6 at row8 col17 →0. Other 6 objects unchanged.
7. Input 21x19, bg7, no obvious divider: color5 component (four horizontal at row5 cols5-8 plus one below at row6 col6) →1. Other 5 absent; color8 and 1 objects unchanged.
8. Input 21x28, bg5, color3 separator L at col6 rows1-6 and row6 cols1-6: color4 upper-right component rows7-9 cols16-19 (11 cells) →3. Similar lower-right 4 component unchanged.
The demos suggest some selected object might relate spatially to a separator or another component, but demos 5 and 7 lack an obvious separator and counterexamples remain. Replacement often equals separator color when a divider exists, but this is not universal. Never generalize from a single motif; test a candidate against all changed and preserved components.
The test grid for that instance had upper objects color1 at rows1-3 cols2 and 20-21; color9 col6 rows1-2 plus left region rows6-10 cols3-4 and row6 cols7-12; color3 objects row3 col7, rows4 col6-7, line col15 rows7-10, pair row7 cols14-15, pair row11 cols5-6, row12 cols11-14; color6 cluster rows2-4 cols13-17; 4 at row3 col11 and pair row10 cols21-22; color5 object rows11-12 cols19-23/19; color7 block rows13-14 cols21-23. Failed output hypotheses were: change color6 cluster to3; additionally change color7 block to9; change color3 vertical line to9; change color7 block to3; change isolated 4 to9; change color7 block to9 again; change color3 vertical object to4; then change isolated 4 and color7 block to9; final submitted variations changing the color3 line and/or isolated 4/color7 cluster. These failures reject those particular predictions, not necessarily each individual component choice in every combination. Current rule unresolved.

## Diagonal-ray task task-9bc5df6e: distinguish ray direction and blockers

### Separate eight-demo run (unresolved; test failed all 8 submissions)
Do not transfer an unverified ray selection rule from other task-9bc5df6e recurrences. This run supplied eight demos; selected outward diagonal rays were drawn in several, but other diagonal-looking motifs remained unchanged. The following exact evidence is useful for filtering hypotheses (0-indexed coordinates):

- Demo 1, 14x16, bg7: extended 6 NW from (7,8) to edge (0,1); extended 4 NE from (7,11) to (3,15); extended 8 SW from (10,8) to (13,5); extended 9 SE from (10,11) to (13,14). Seed cells retained.
- Demo 2, 29x8, bg9: extended color5 NW from (16,2) through (15,1),(14,0). Other nearby color1/4 cells did not produce obvious rays.
- Demo 3, 18x6, bg5: extended 9 from (16,1) down-left to (17,0); all else unchanged.
- Demo 4, 6x6: no changes, despite a small mixed-color diagonal-like cluster near the upper-right corner.
- Demo 5, 11x12, bg5: extended 9 NW from (5,2) to (0,7); extended 3 SE from (8,2) through (9,3),(10,4). Preserve the neighboring mixed marker shape.
- Demo 6, 18x13: no changes to the small top-edge cluster (including 5,6,2); do not extend every apparent diagonal.
- Demo 7, 19x21, bg4: extended 2 upward-right from (2,12) to (0,14); extended 8 SW from (5,9) to (14,0); extended 5 SE from (5,12) to (13,20). Color9 near this motif stayed unchanged.
- Demo 8, 15x5, bg7: extended 3 SE from (2,3) to (3,4), preserving other cells.

Test was 13x23, bg2, with diagonal pairs: 8 at (2,14),(3,15); 7 at (2,17),(3,16); 5 at (4,15),(5,14); 3 at (4,16),(5,17). Eight test submissions were all rejected. Guesses included no rays; all four likely outward rays (8 NW, 7 NE, 5 SW, 3 SE); pairs of only 8/7 top rays or only 5/3 lower rays; and several subsets/direction variants. Therefore do not treat the intuitive four-ray completion as confirmed for this particular run. Reassess which endpoints/rays are selected by a cross-example structural predicate, including negative examples demo4/6 and unchanged color9 in demo7, before using this task ID again. This run remains unresolved; no submitted test grid should be reused as a validated answer.

### Older confirmed/other recurring variants

- One prior run had colored diagonal seed pairs/branches extend in straight rays through empty background to the grid boundary; direction inferred from the outward-facing endpoint(s), preserving seeds and unrelated cells. A separate run had the test unchanged because the next diagonal cell was a non-background blocker. See the details below; this does not establish the selector for every recurrence.

#### Current confirmed background-ray run (task-9bc5df6e)

- One confirmed run: colored diagonal seed pairs/branches extend in a straight diagonal ray away from the local motif through background cells to the boundary, preserving seed cells and unrelated content. In another run, demos showed background-only diagonal rays, and accepted test remained unchanged because the continuation next cell was occupied by non-background color 2. Extend only through background; do not overwrite blockers.

- **Confirmed two-demo variant, accepted 26x27 test:** Both demos show diagonal motif arms continuing outward as same-colored rays through the uniform background to the grid edge, while retaining all original motif cells and all unrelated colors. Demo 1 (22x11, background 1): color 2 ray extends NW from seed (12,5) to (7,0); color 3 ray extends NE from (12,8) to (10,10), retaining its diagonal motif cells (12,8),(13,7); color 4 ray extends SW from (15,5) to (20,0). Demo 2 (27x10, background 6): color 7 extends NW from (19,3) to (16,0); color 0 extends SW from (22,3) to (25,0); color 4 extends SE from (22,6) to (25,9). Coordinates are zero-indexed; rays stop at the boundary and never recolor occupied cells. The accepted test (26x27, background 8) had color-9 diagonal seed pair (16,21),(17,22); extend NW from the outward endpoint (16,21), filling (15,20) through (0,5) with 9. Preserve the adjacent 1/5 motif at rows 17–18, cols 22–23, original 9s, and every other cell. This confirms ray continuation in multiple directions and with distinct colors for this demonstrated variant, but does not resolve the selector for all task-9bc5df6e recurrences; continue to distinguish from the documented unresolved eight-demo variant and blocked/no-op cases.


- **Additional accepted no-op variant (26x23 test):** Demos 1 (27x8, bg1) and 2 (9x19, bg5) contained only small mixed-color motifs and were unchanged. Demo 3 (9x15, bg3) had a same-color diagonal pair of 9s at (6,10),(7,11) in 0-indexed coordinates; the output continued that diagonal NW from (6,10), filling (5,9),(4,8),(3,7),(2,6),(1,5),(0,4), and left the mixed-color neighboring shape at rows 7-8, cols 11-12 untouched. The accepted test had only a 2x2 mixed-color block at rows 19-20, cols 2-3 (`[[1,7],[1,4]]`), with no same-color diagonal pair to extend, so the correct output was exactly the input unchanged. This confirms not to draw rays from arbitrary mixed motifs or vertical/horizontal same-color adjacencies. ## Unresolved task-d569e96a: three-example recoloring decomposition (2026-09)
Three 7x7 demonstrations map input color-8 patterns on color-0 background into colors 1,2,3,4 while preserving zero cells. The rule/selector is unresolved; the paired structures appear decomposed spatially in ways that are not captured by simply coloring connected components or fixed quadrants. Exact pairs (rows compactly listed, each digit a cell):

1. Input `0008800 / 8888800 / 0880880 / 0888800 / 0008800 / 0000000 / 0000000`; output `0011000 / 3311400 / 0320440 / 0221100 / 0001100 / 0000000 / 0000000`.
2. Input `0800800 / 8800880 / 0880880 / 0880880 / 0088000 / 0008000 / 0000000`; output `0200400 / 2200440 / 0110110 / 0110110 / 0033000 / 0003000 / 0000000`.
3. Input `8880000 / 8888000 / 8808000 / 0888000 / 0000000 / 0000000 / 0000000`; output `1140000 / 1144000 / 3302000 / 0322000 / 0000000 / 0000000 / 0000000`.

Test `0880880 / 8888880 / 0880800 / 0088800 / 0000000 / 0000000 / 0000000` was submitted eight times; every prediction was rejected. Failed outputs tried multiple guesses of spatial blocks/regions to colors 1–4 (one used color 5), including fixed left/right and lower-region assignments, so none are validated. On recurrence, first tabulate every input-8 coordinate and output color for all demos; investigate whether overlapping/stacked shapes or a motif encoding governs coloring rather than connected components. Preserve zero cells unless demos prove otherwise. Do not recycle failed test grids or infer a palette mapping by visual intuition alone.

## Confirmed task-202106df: recover rectangular zeroed patch by vertical reflection (accepted, 2026-09)
The input is a 24x24 patterned grid with a rectangular all-zero occlusion. Restore the hidden rectangle by reflecting the corresponding cells across the vertical centerline: for each zero at `(r,c)` in the rectangular hole, copy the original input value at `(r,23-c)`. Preserve every nonzero input cell and all dimensions. In the accepted test, the 3x3 hole at rows 9–11, cols 14–16 was restored as `[[6,8,4],[5,9,4],[8,9,4]]` (each row matches its mirrored source cells at cols 9–7). Two demos confirmed rectangular holes of varying sizes: demo 1 had an 8x5 hole at rows 15–22, cols 5–9; output was the 8x5 reflected patch. Demo 2 had a 4x3 hole at rows 4–7, cols 10–12; output was the 4x3 reflected patch. The output consists of the hidden region only, not the completed full grid. First test guess mistakenly returned the full grid; after two demos established crop-and-reflect, the 3x3 patch submission was accepted. On recurrence, identify the all-zero rectangle, reflect horizontally from the opposite side, and emit exactly its HxW patch. Verify coordinate mapping and output shape carefully.

## Unresolved task-f762568d: diagonal marker/ray construction (5 demos, test exhausted)

A five-demo recurrence with sparse color-1 and color-6 singleton markers on a uniform background appeared to draw some diagonal links/rays, but the selection and exact direction/extent rule was not resolved. The 19x16 test exhausted all 8 submissions; do not reuse any submitted grid or treat these hypotheses as rules. This is specifically a warning against assuming every diagonal marker or every same-color pair activates a ray.

Demo evidence (0-indexed):
- Demo 1 (9x9, bg4): 1 markers at (2,1) and (7,6); output draws a bounded down-right 1 diagonal joining them, adding (3,2),(4,3),(5,4),(6,5). No 6 marker present.
- Demo 2 (8x11, bg8): 6 at (3,4) is extended along its NW-SE diagonal to both boundaries (from (0,1) through (7,8)); 1s at (1,6),(6,1) are joined on their down-left/up-right diagonal by filling (2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2). Note that the 1 connector crosses a location that was background and is not the 6 ray's same coordinate line in this orientation.
- Demo 3 (9x12, bg4): 1s at (1,7),(7,1) are joined along down-left diagonal, filling (2,6) through (6,2). The 6 at (6,7) remains unchanged, a counterexample to extending every 6 marker.
- Demo 4 (15x12, bg5): output adds diagonal 1/6 cells along several lines, preserving all original markers. For example 1 pair at (3,1),(9,7) is joined down-right through rows 4–8; there are also 6 marker/ray structures, including a long down-left progression from near the top-right to the lower-left edge and another reaching from a lower marker toward an edge. This demo is not sufficient to identify which 6 directions activate; audit the original pair cell-by-cell before generalizing.
- Demo 5 (15x16, bg8): 1 markers at (2,2),(3,12),(11,11),(14,3) and 6 markers at (1,8),(9,9),(10,1),(14,13). Output connects the first two 1 markers down-right across rows 2–3; extends some 1/6 diagonal patterns but leaves other plausible continuations absent. In particular a 6 line through (9,9) is extended up-right/down-left along its diagonal; 6 at (1,8) proceeds down-right; 6 at (10,1) extends down-left to the edge; and the marker (14,13) remains without a conspicuous continuation. This mixed activation is a crucial negative constraint.

Test (19x16, bg4) markers: 1s at (2,2),(4,14),(10,10),(17,9); 6s at (4,4),(6,6),(7,14),(15,2). Eight rejected submissions tried: (1) connecting 1s/rays only in intuitive SE directions; (2) blanket full anti-diagonal 6 lines plus 1 line; (3) only bounded aligned 1 and 6 pairs; (4) full 6 diagonals in another orientation; (5) main-diagonal 1/6 continuation guesses; (6) broad bidirectional 6 rays; (7) bounded marker linking / mixed ray selection; (8) broad diagonal 6 completion plus bounded 1 link. None is validated, and failures indicate selector/direction assumptions—not merely palette or grid dimensions—were unsupported. On recurrence, tabulate every changed and preserved diagonal line in each demo with exact orientation, endpoints, nearest object relationships, and edge direction; derive a selector replaying all five before submitting. If no such rule is established, avoid recycling guesses; demos have a cost and the test attempt cap is finite.

## Related skills

For pattern-specific guidance, consult `arc-prototype-stamping` for motif propagation and `arc-striped-panel-pair-count` for panel partition/count mappings. This skill provides general demonstration analysis and validation; specialized skills provide particular transformations.
